extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (litigators and prosecutors), judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes and explains Federal Circuit and PTAB legal standards across patentability, disclosure, novelty, obviousness, claim construction, infringement, remedies, PTO/PTAB procedure, and design-patent analysis as reflected in recent case law. Useful as a reference for applying current doctrinal tests and courtroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step one — directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea if it does not amount to a computer-specific technical improvement; merely identifying, analyzing, and presenting data, or improving a user experience without a specific mechanism, is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For computer-based technologies, courts look for claimed advances focused on 'an improvement in computer technologies, rather than the mere use of computers.' Avoid characterizing claims at an impermissibly high level of generality. (International Business Machines v. Zillow; AI Visualize v. Nuance; Contour IP v. GoPro.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two — inventive concept / 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Alice step two, a claim must recite elements or combinations that transform the nature of the claim beyond routine, conventional, or well-known elements, i.e., something 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require specific, discrete implementations and will reject conclusory allegations of inventiveness that do not tie to claim text or specification. Use of conventional technologies (e.g., GPS on phones) generally does not supply an inventive concept. (AI Visualize; Beteiro; IBM v. Zillow.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-technology improvement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For software/computer claims, the claimed advance must be an improvement in computer technologies themselves (a technological improvement) rather than mere use of computers as tools to implement an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely create virtual views, manipulate data, or perform longstanding economic activities via generic computing are likely ineligible. Emphasize specific technological means (e.g., parallel video streams with bandwidth-saving transfer) when arguing eligibility. (AI Visualize; Beteiro; Contour IP v. GoPro.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem with result-focused functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite result-focused functional language without specifics on how the results are achieved are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete mechanisms or specific steps/implementations in the specification and claims; avoid broad 'do X to achieve Y' recitations without structural/technical detail. (Beteiro.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding impermissibly high-level claim characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will reject treating claims at an overbroad, high level of generality when determining subject-matter eligibility; correct characterization focuses on the specific technological means claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and argue construction to show concrete technological improvements rather than sweeping goals. (Contour IP v. GoPro.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine — content vs communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed matter doctrine applies to 'matter claimed for what it communicates' (the content or information), not to mere communication mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim involving communication is not excluded simply because it sends or receives data; the doctrine only bars patentability when the claimed matter is the communicated content itself. Program-code limitations that are silent as to content may not be barred. (IOENGINE v. Ingenico.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Party presentation and § 282 presumption of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should generally act as neutral arbiters and are limited to deciding issues framed and litigated by the parties; they should not resolve patentability grounds (e.g., § 101) sua sponte where parties did not litigate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patents are presumptively valid under 35 U.S.C. § 282, courts must require challengers to present clear and convincing evidence on issues not raised by the parties. (Astellas Pharma v. Sandoz.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness — claim limitations are conditions, not options
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations recite conditions that must be met; two limitations are not contradictory merely because one lists options that the other narrows, so long as both requirements can be met simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness requires true contradiction; courts will not automatically find indefiniteness because of dependent/independent claim placement. (Maxell v. Amperex.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness — need for measurement method when techniques diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term that requires a quantitative measurement (e.g., particle size) is indefinite if the specification does not indicate which conventional measurement technique should be used and different conventional techniques produce meaningfully different results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide measurement methodology or clear specification guidance when numerical ranges are claimed; absence of reliable evidence that techniques differ may defeat an indefiniteness challenge. (Janssen v. Teva.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionally claimed structural elements — permissible functional construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim limitations may be construed functionally rather than by rigid physical boundaries; functional constructions can differ in their physical manifestation across different claims without creating indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will perform claim-by-claim constructions and may accept functional constructions that do not specify exact physical dimensions if the functional boundaries are sufficiently informing. (Vascular Solutions v. Medtronic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description — broad range can support narrower subrange
rubrics_metrics.description: A broadly disclosed range in the specification can provide written-description support for a narrower claimed subrange where it would be clear to a skilled artisan that the subrange describes the same invention, especially in predictable arts and where endpoints are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure specification discloses endpoints or overlapping ranges and indicate predictability of the technology to support later-claimed subranges. (Rai Strategic Holdings v. Philip Morris.)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar and secret commercial use (pre-AIA/AIA §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales of products made by a secret process can trigger the on-sale bar (§ 102(a)) even if the process was secret; the AIA textual changes did not alter the settled meaning that such sales can defeat novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that secret commercial exploitation that results in sales may put a critical date at risk; rely on Helsinn and related precedent. (Celanese v. ITC.)

rubrics_metrics.name: §102(b)(2)(B) 'public disclosure' exception is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA § 102(b)(2)(B) 'public disclosure' exception only covers disclosures that result in the subject matter of the invention being publicly disclosed; purely private sales/messages that do not disclose to the public do not trigger the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private transfers of information or private sales typically will not create the one-year grace period under § 102(b)(2)(B). (Sanho v. Kaijet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — motivation to combine must be supported (no bare common sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of obviousness based on combining references requires evidence that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine the references for a reason; mere statements of 'common sense' or conclusory testimony are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide articulation of why references would be combined and evidence supporting motivation and reasonable expectation of success. (Virtek v. Assembly Guidance Systems; Virtek; Aligned Vision discussions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR-driven obviousness analysis — consider POSA creativity and interrelated teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness analysis must account for the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA), including their ordinary creativity and the interrelated teachings of prior art; courts must not apply rigid or overly narrow approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mechanical comparison; evaluate whether an ordinarily creative POSA would combine teachings even if the prior art lacks explicit overlap. (Janssen v. Teva.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure 'teaches away' only when it explicitly discourages the modification or alternative; the mere existence of a preferred or optimal value does not necessarily teach away other values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate explicit discouragement or showing that POSA would be deterred from the claimed modification to establish teaching away. (Janssen v. Teva.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia — such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, industry praise, copying, and licensing activity — are relevant to the obviousness inquiry and must be properly instructed to the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the trial record and jury instructions include all relevant secondary considerations presented by the parties; omission can be reversible error. (Inline Plastics v. Lacerta.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — per-claim analysis and non-exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be construed claim-by-claim; independent claims can vary in how they claim disclosed subject matter and need not be totally consistent with other independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform individualized construction rather than imposing a uniform physical boundary across all claims; avoid assuming claims are mutually exclusive without detailed analysis. (Vascular Solutions v. Medtronic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter and program-code limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims recite program code or information, the printed matter doctrine only applies if the claim is directed to the content the matter communicates; a claim silent as to the contents of code may avoid the doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to claim technical functionality or structure rather than pure informational content to avoid printed matter issues. (IOENGINE v. Ingenico.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical/biotech obviousness — expectation of success and specific evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: In pharmaceutical or clinical settings, obviousness findings require attention to whether a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success when combining references; mere speculation that a combination yields known dosages or outcomes is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data, rationale, or convincing expert testimony demonstrating why a POSA would expect success; courts will scrutinize clinical expectations closely. (Salix; Janssen discussions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR institution and 'significant relationship' under General Plastics/Valve
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'significant relationship' between parties can bar institution in some contexts, but court-ordered pretrial coordination alone does not create a significant relationship if the parties have different accused products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere coordination from deeper relationships that would implicate institution tests; factual showing of different accused products may defeat a 'significant relationship' objection. (American Honda v. Neo Wireless.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Director review / Delegated Review Panel usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Director review decisions may be referred to an independent Delegated Review Panel (DRP); the DRP mechanism is available for institutional review of PTAB decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for Director-level review and DRP procedures in institution-denial contexts. (DK Crown Holdings Director Decision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to appeal PTAB decisions — injury-in-fact requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A party appealing a PTAB decision must establish Article III standing by showing an injury in fact; allegations of speculative future infringement or vague collateral consequences are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate concrete plans or substantial risk of infringement or clearly articulated collateral consequences to establish standing on appeal. (Allgenesis v. Cloudbreak.)

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB jurisdiction after statutory timing deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB's failure to issue a Final Written Decision by a statutory deadline (e.g., 18 months) does not necessarily deprive the Board of authority to issue that decision later absent specified statutory consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness violations alone may not nullify PTAB decisions; analyze statutory text and legislative history for specific consequences. (Purdue Pharma v. Collegium.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent obviousness — Graham-based framework (overruling Rosen-Durling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness for design patents should follow a Graham-type analysis: consider (1) scope and content of the prior art (analogous art), (2) differences between the claimed design and the prior art (visual appearance from ordinary designer perspective), and (3) the level of ordinary skill (a designer of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ordinary designers would have been motivated to modify prior art to create the same overall visual appearance; secondary considerations remain relevant. This replaces the rigid Rosen-Durling two-step test. (LKQ v. GM en banc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents — analogous art scope
rubrics_metrics.description: At minimum, 'analogous art' includes prior art from the same field of endeavor as the article of manufacture claimed; other art may be analogous depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden prior-art consideration appropriately in design cases while focusing on visual comparison from a designer's perspective. (LKQ v. GM.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorneys' fees under § 285 and parallel IPR proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a defendant voluntarily pursues IPR proceedings in parallel with district litigation, courts may decline to award attorneys' fees under § 285 for fees incurred in the IPR, given the voluntary nature and differing procedural posture of IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts awarding § 285 fees should consider whether the challenged fees were incurred in proceedings the court did not oversee and whether the party was compelled to pursue IPR. (Dragon IP v. DISH; note dissenting view.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal jurisdiction — purposeful direction and effects in forum
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that purposefully directs activities at a forum (e.g., via a program that, if unopposed, would remove third-party listings from the forum's marketplace) can be subject to specific personal jurisdiction in that forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the defendant's actions were purposefully directed to the forum and whether exercising jurisdiction is reasonable under the circumstances. (SnapRays v. Lighting Defense Group.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert qualification — no timing requirement tied to date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert need not possess the requisite ordinary skill in the art 'at the time of the alleged invention' as a precondition to qualify; lack of such timing goes to credibility rather than admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to expert admissibility should focus on methodology/reliability (Daubert) rather than a strict timing-based qualification. (Osseo Imaging v. Planmeca.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert methodology — reliance on documents vs independent testing
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert's failure to perform independent testing or simulation does not automatically render testimony unreliable if the expert reasonably relies on schematics, technical documents, and other materials created by those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts may opine based on reliable documentary and technical sources; courts should not require independent testing in every case to admit testimony. (ParkerVision v. Qualcomm.)
